newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says open to talks with Syria on all issues.
newsitem.headline: Israel says open to talks with Syria on all issues.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants the resumption of peace talks with Syria on all issues and without preconditions, his spokesman said on Sunday.
"The prime minister says that in negotiations with Syria, each side can come to the table to raise all issues they want with no preconditions," spokesman Shai Bazak told Reuters.
Bazak took issue with a report published in the French daily Le Figaro on Saturday that said Netanyahu had ruled out negotiation over the fate of the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.

"The things published in Le Figaro are not exact and are not quoted exactly," Bazak said. "It is possible to talk about every issue that the sides raise. We do not tell the Syrians on which issues we can talk."
"We want negotiations to resume. The stance that Israel will bring to the talks will be that the Golan is important for Israel's security," Bazak said.
The comments printed in Le Figaro drew sharp condemnation from Damascus on Sunday.

"This obstinate position would close the doors for efforts which are supposed to start again with the beginning of the second term of office of U.S. President Bill Clinton," the state-owned Syrian daily Al-Baath said.
President Clinton, whose country has sponsored five years of sporadic peace talks between arch-foes Israel and Syria, will begin his second term on Monday.

On the heels of an Israeli redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron that revived moribund peace moves between Israel and the PLO, analysts have turned their attention to the long-stalled Israeli-Syrian negotiations.

The talks have been blocked over the fate of the Golan, which Israel seized from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war. Syria demands a full Israeli withdrawal in exchange for peace. Netanyahu also wants all of the strategic plateau.
Bazak again rejected the Syrian demand that peace talks resume from the point where Israel's previous government left them last March.
"We have said in the past that this government is committed to signed agreements. There have not been signed agreements on the Syrian track since the (1991) Madrid conference," he said.
Israel's previous centre-left government, ousted by the right-wing Netanyahu in May, said it was willing to make at least a partial withdrawal from the Golan but signed no deals with Damascus.
